## Coordinates for the Paulis {#sec-paulis}

Finite groups are among the simplest objects in mathematics, and among
the most quietly powerful. A group is a finite collection of things with
a single operation that combines any two of them into a third. The rule
that gives the idea its force is closure: combine two members and you
land on a member again, every time, so you can go on combining forever
without ever leaving the set or enlarging it. The smallest example worth
naming is $\mathbb{Z}_2$, two elements $0$ and $1$ combined by addition
modulo two, with $0 + 1 = 1$ and $1 + 1 = 0$. A light switch, a coin
turned over and over: two states and one move that flips between them,
with nowhere else to go.

Here is the move that makes groups so useful, and it is the one to hold
onto. You can *represent* a group by matrices: attach a matrix to each
element so that multiplying the matrices reproduces the group's own
operation. A representation is the bridge from an abstract group to
concrete linear algebra. For $\mathbb{Z}_2$ it can be as small as two
$2 \times 2$ matrices,
$$
0 \;\longmapsto\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
1 \;\longmapsto\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
The first does nothing; the second swaps the two entries it acts on, a
flip. Multiply the flip by itself and the swaps cancel, returning the
identity, exactly as $1 + 1 = 0$ in the group. Before reading on, it is
worth confirming for yourself that this really is a representation: it
has to turn every sum in the group into the matching product of
matrices. There are only four sums to check, so run the identity and the
flip through all of them and watch each one land on the nose. Addition
modulo two has become matrix multiplication, and that translation is so
fruitful that the representation theory of finite groups is a deep and
thoroughly mapped field in its own right.

We built $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and its representation as a rehearsal, because
the qubit is one honest step up from it. Read $\mathbb{Z}_2$ as the
arithmetic of a single classical bit: the only move is to flip it or
leave it, one coordinate over $\{0,1\}$, and its exact representation was
the pair $\{I, \text{flip}\}$. One coordinate, no phase. That is the
whole classical system.

Passing to a qubit adds exactly one coordinate. Beside the classical
question "does it flip?" the quantum world sets a second one with no
classical echo: "does it pick up a phase?" A qubit's elementary moves are
labelled by both answers at once, a little vector
$$
(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}_2^2,
$$
with $a$ the flip and $b$ the phase. There are exactly four,
$$
(0,0), \quad (1,0), \quad (0,1), \quad (1,1),
$$
and this two-coordinate space over $\mathbb{Z}_2$, the classical bit
widened by a phase axis, is the qubit's *phase space*.

Each vector names one operator we have been drawing since the Bloch ball.
Nothing done is the identity; a flip alone is $X$; a phase alone is $Z$; a
flip and a phase together is $Y$:
$$
(0,0) \mapsto I, \quad (1,0) \mapsto X, \quad (0,1) \mapsto Z, \quad
(1,1) \mapsto Y.
$$
These are the *Pauli matrices*,
$$
X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
with the identity $I$ at the centre, and they are the $x$, $y$, $z$ axes
of the Bloch ball we have been drawing all along. The four Paulis are
nothing more than the four points of the phase space, written as
matrices.

The group law carries across unchanged: to combine two operators, add
their vectors entry by entry, modulo two, exactly as we added in
$\mathbb{Z}_2$. A flip $(1,0)$ then a phase $(0,1)$ gives $(1,1)$, which
is $Y$, a flip and a phase at once. Multiplying Paulis has become adding
phase-space vectors, the same move as before, one dimension wider.

One thing is new, and it is the thing the rest of the post turns on.
Multiply the actual matrices and an extra phase appears that the vectors
never see. Set $XZ$ against $ZX$: both reach the same vector $(1,1)$, yet
the matrices differ by a sign, $XZ = -ZX$. Adding vectors records *which*
operator you land on and quietly loses the phase you gathered getting
there. So the Paulis are not quite a representation of $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$.
They are a representation up to a phase, a *projective* one. The classical
bit had nothing of the sort; the new coordinate arrived with a phase
riding on top of it.

That phase is the one genuinely new ingredient the quantum problem hands
us, and naming it well is most of the work ahead. Carry it as a function
sitting on top of the phase space, a single phase pinned to each vector.
Then anything built from these operators, a channel included, comes apart
into two clean pieces: a rule that moves the phase-space vectors around,
and this phase function riding along above them. Those two pieces, and
nothing heavier, are all we need to take the qubit apart.

None of this leaned on there being two levels. Give the system $d$ levels
instead of two and the same story unfolds with more dots. The Paulis grow
into $d^2$ operators, the *Weyl operators* $\mathbf{w}(\eta)$, each tagged
by a pair $\eta = (a, b)$ whose entries now run $0, 1, \ldots, d - 1$
rather than just $0$ and $1$. They still form a basis of every
$d \times d$ matrix, so a channel is fixed by what it does to them; they
still multiply by adding tags, now modulo $d$; and they still do so only
up to a trailing phase, now a $d$-th root of unity $\omega = e^{2\pi i/d}$
in place of a sign. The tags no longer fill a $2 \times 2$ square but a
$d \times d$ grid, the plane we will write $\mathbb{F}_d^2$.

One label stands apart on that grid. The origin $(0,0)$ is the identity,
the trace direction every channel in our class must leave untouched. That
leaves $d^2 - 1$ nonzero labels, the directions that can genuinely be
forgotten, and they are exactly the $d^2 - 1$ dimensions we counted on the
Bloch ball, come back as the nonzero points of a finite grid. (One feature
of the grid will matter later: it behaves like a full number system, where
you can divide as freely as you add and multiply, only when $d$ is prime.
We will not need division until the labels start moving, and the explicit
shift-and-phase recipe for $\mathbf{w}(\eta)$ is one fold away.)

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>The Weyl operators explicitly, and why $d$ must be prime</summary>
```

Fix $d$ levels, $|0\rangle$ through $|d-1\rangle$. Two elementary moves
generate everything. The first is a *shift* that bumps every level up by
one and wraps around at the top, $X\colon|j\rangle \mapsto |j+1\rangle$,
the higher-dimensional bit-flip. The second is a *phase kick* that
multiplies level $j$ by a $d$-th root of unity,
$Z\colon|j\rangle \mapsto \omega^{\,j}|j\rangle$ with
$\omega = e^{2\pi i/d}$, the higher-dimensional phase-flip. Applying $a$
shifts and $b$ phase kicks gives the Weyl operator
$\mathbf{w}(a,b) \sim X^a Z^b$, fixed up to a phase convention we never
need; there are $d^2$ of them, one for each label $(a,b)$ with $a$ and
$b$ taken modulo $d$. At $d = 2$ they are just the four Paulis renamed.

Multiply two and the labels add, up to that same phase:
$\mathbf{w}(\eta)\,\mathbf{w}(\xi) = (\text{phase}) \cdot \mathbf{w}(\eta + \xi)$.
The labels add exactly, but the operators reproduce that addition only up
to a phase, which is why the assignment is called a *projective*
representation of the group of labels; we never need the phase's exact
form. As for the primality: the integers modulo a prime form a *field*
$\mathbb{F}_d$, in which division works as cleanly as addition,
subtraction and multiplication. We will need to divide by labels, not
merely add them, once the labels start moving around the plane, and
division behaves only when $d$ is prime.

```{=html}
</details>
```

That is the whole stage: a plane of labels $\mathbb{F}_d^2$, with a phase
trailing along whenever you multiply. Everything left in this post plays
out on it. The channels we are about to single out do just two things to
this plane. They *relabel* it, sending each point to another by a single
linear map, each axis to an axis. And at each label they pin on a number
of their own, a phase that is also allowed to shrink in size. That
attached number is where forgetting will live, and following it around
the plane is how we hunt down the long roots. Time to meet the channels.
